Q478.1.2.1.p: An adulteress is forced to eat out of her lover's skull.

Q478.1.3.p: An adulteress is punished by having the skeleton of her former lover hung in her room.

Q478.1.4.p: An adulteress is forced to have her lover's head placed before her at meals.

Q478.2.r: (Cf. Q241, Q478.) *Chauvin VIII 162 No. 170; Malone PMLA XLIII 430; Gibb History of the Forty Vezirs 331ff.; Irish myth: Cross.
Q478.2.p: An adulteress is forced to eat together with a dog as punishment.

Q478.3.r: (Cf. Q241, Q523.3.) Malone PMLA XLIII 405—430 passim.
Q478.3.p: An adulteress is forced to eat what a dog has left behind.

Q478.4.p: A father or husband punishes a daughter by using fat rendered from her mutilated corpse to cook with and to make candles.

Q478.5.p: A punishment in which the offender must eat ashes instead of normal food.

Q478.5.1.p: A punishment in which the guilty person is forced to eat ashes or coal mixed into their food.

Q481.p: A princess or queen is forced to run an inn as a humiliating punishment.

Q482.r: (Cf. A181, H465.) Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 319f., O’Suilleabhain 53; Missouri French: Carrière; Greek: Grote I 54; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/48, z-G. 3/1386).
Q482.p: A person of noble birth is punished by being made to do lowly servant's work.

Q482.1.p: A princess is punished by being made to work as a servant.

Q482.1.1.p: A second wife, who was a slave, is made to work as a servant as punishment.

Q482.2.r: Irish myth: Cross. Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 101.
Q482.2.p: A queen is put to work in the kitchen and mistreated by a butcher.

Q482.2.1.p: A queen forced into menial service in the kitchen is rescued by her son.

Q482.2.2.p: A queen is ordered to go live in a woodcutter's house as a servant.

Q482.3.p: After death, a nobleman must continue to serve as a menial servant.

Q482.4.p: A cast-out wife must sit at the horse-block of the palace, telling her story to each newcomer and offering to carry them inside.

Q482.5.p: A queen is made to scare crows away from the fields as punishment.

Q482.6.p: A man is punished by being forced to do women's work.

Q483.p: A princess is punished by being made to sell goods in the market.

Q483.1.p: A condemned queen is exposed in leather on the market place.

Q484.p: As punishment for adultery, a husband fondles his second wife in front of the first wife.

Q485.p: A person of noble birth is punished by being made to live in a hovel.

Q485.1.p: A princess who has married a lowly hero is made to live in the slave quarters.

Q486.p: A criminal's property is destroyed as punishment.

Q486.1.p: A criminal's house is burned down as punishment.

Q486.1.1.p: A sinful city is burned down as punishment.

Q487.r: (Cf. Q241.) Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 49; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
Q487.p: A wife guilty of adultery is made by her husband to wear a dress of coarse cloth, with only her undefiled parts covered in gold brocade, so her disgrace is displayed publicly.

Q488.p: A person is punished by having their hair cut off as a humiliation.

Q488.1.p: A goat that lies is punished by having only half of its coat shorn off.

Q488.2.p: A person is punished by having their head shaved completely.

Q491.p: A dead body is treated with disrespect as a punishment for the person who died.

Q491.1.p: A person is given a shameful burial as a punishment, even after death.

Q491.1.1.r: (Cf. Q274.) Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 143 No. 1720.
Q491.1.1.p: A swindler is punished after death by being buried on a dungheap instead of in a proper grave.

Q491.1.2.p: As punishment for desecrating holy places, a person is given a disgraceful burial in a deserted barn.

Q491.2.p: The corpse of a man who owed debts is beaten with a whip as punishment.

Q491.3.p: The devil beats the corpse of a wicked man.

Q491.4.r: Scala Celi 74b No. 426; Herbert III 99 No. 65, 666 No. 261; Irish: Beal XXI 327, O’Suilleabhain 74.
Q491.4.p: Toads and snakes eat the corpse of a rich man while it lies in its grave.

Q491.5.r: (Cf. Q478.1.2.) DeCock Volkssage 96ff.; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q491.5.p: A skull is used as a drinking cup.

Q491.6.r: (Cf. Q211.) Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Greek: Grote I 275, 278.
Q491.6.p: The corpse of a murderer is mutilated as punishment.

Q491.6.1.p: The corpse of a murderer is cut into pieces as punishment.

Q491.7.p: As punishment, a dead body is thrown into a river.

Q492.r: Spargo Virgil the Necromancer (Cambridge, Mass., 1934) 199ff.; *Oertel Studien zur vgl. Literaturgeschichte VIII 113; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
Q492.p: A magician, angry at ill-treatment, puts out all the city's lights, which can only be relit from the naked body of a woman in the public square; the woman is thus forced to relight them, and none can be relit until all have applied their torches.

Q493.p: A person is punished by being saddled and ridden like a horse.

Q493.1.p: An adulterous wife is transformed into a mare and then saddled and ridden with stirrups.

Q494.p: A person is punished by losing their social rank or standing.

Q494.1.p: A king who defies a saint loses his royal line, so the kingship is taken away from his family.

Q494.1.1.p: A king who is uncharitable to others loses his power.

Q494.2.p: A person is removed from the priesthood as a punishment, losing their social standing.

Q495.p: A punishment in which the offender's body is exposed in a shameful way, so that they are humiliated in public.

Q495.1.r: (Cf. Q321.) Type 902*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 902*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 902*; Russian: Andrejev No. 902*; Japanese: Ikeda.
Q495.1.p: A lazy wife is punished by being carried naked, wrapped in a bundle of straw, to a wedding.

Q497.p: A man's beard is shaved off as the punishment for committing murder.

Q497.1.p: A man's moustache is pulled out by way of punishment.

Q499.p: A miscellaneous group of humiliating punishments that do not fit the other categories.

Q499.1.p: A punishment in which the offender is forced to give a humiliating kiss.

Q499.1.1.p: A humiliating punishment in which the offender is made to kiss a leper.

Q499.2.p: A punishment in which the offender is put to death in a humiliating way.

Q499.2.1.p: A humiliating death is the punishment for adultery.

Q499.2.2.p: A humiliating death is the punishment for taking a concubine.

Q499.3.p: The sacrament is refused to a person as punishment for desecrating a holy place.

Q499.4.p: A person is punished by being satirized, that is, mocked in verse or song, for refusing a request.

Q499.4.1.p: A person is punished by being satirized for breaking a treaty.

Q499.5.p: Clergy who are in debt are forbidden to hold church offices.

Q499.6.p: A person must do penance for three and a half years for eating horse meat.

Q499.7.p: A marriage forced on a person as a humiliating punishment.

Q499.8.p: As a humiliating penance, a king must rub his nose five times on a red-hot griddle.

Q500.p: A group of punishments that involve long, drawn-out suffering rather than a quick end.

Q501.p: A punishment of constant torture that never stops or lets up.

Q501.1.r: Reinach Revue Archéologique 1903 (4) Series I 154ff.; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 78 n. 3.
Q501.1.p: The punishment of Sisyphus: he must keep rolling a great stone up a hill, and it always falls back down before he reaches the top.

Q501.2.r: Reinach Revue Archéologique 1903 (4) series I 154ff.; *Frazer Pausanias V 392; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus II 154 n. 2; Jewish: *Neuman.
Q501.2.p: Punishment of Tantalus: the sufferer stands in water that always drains away from his thirsty lips, while fruit branches spring away from his hands and a stone hangs over his head that never quite falls.

Q501.2.1.p: A hungry man tries to pick fruit, but it flies out of his reach as a punishment.

Q501.2.2.p: As punishment, delicious food fills with maggots just as the man is about to eat it.

Q501.3.p: Punishment of Loki: a serpent hangs above him and continually drips venom into his face.

Q501.4.r: (Punishment for theft of fire.) Greek: *W. Schmid Untersuchungen zum gefesselten Prometheus (Stuttgart, 1929), Fox 13, *Frazer Apollodorus I 228 n. 2; Jewish: Neuman.
Q501.4.p: Punishment of Prometheus: he is chained to a mountain while an eagle feeds on his organs, which regrow each night.

Q501.5.p: Punishment of Ixion: he is tied to a wheel that turns endlessly.

Q501.6.p: Punishment of Io: she is turned into a cow and a gadfly chases her without end.

Q501.7.p: Punishment in which the sufferer is endlessly thirsty and never gets relief.

Q501.7.1.p: A man who accepts Christianity is punished by being given salted food and no drink.

Q501.8.p: Punishment of endless humming or singing, imposed for asking for something too much or too immoderately.

Q501.9.p: A spirit in hell is condemned to bathe people endlessly.

Q502.p: Punishment in which the sufferer must wander without rest.

Q502.1.r: (Cf. Q221.3.) Type 754**; **L. Neubaur Die Sage vom Ewigen Jude@2 (Leipzig, 1893); **Zirus Ahasverus, der Ewige Jude (Stoff- und Motivgeschichte der deutschen Literatur No. 6 [Berlin, 1930]); Gielen de Wandelende Jood (Amsterdam, 1931); *K. Nyrop Den evige Jøde (København, 1907); **Neubaur Zs. f. Vksk. XXII 33, Zentralblatt für Bibliothekswesen XXVIII 495ff.; *Dübe Zs. F. Vksk. XVII 143; *Bolte ibid. XIX 308; G. Paris. Légendes du moyen âge@2 (1904) 149ff.; *Fb “Jerusalems skomager” II 40, IV 246a; *Wehrhan 50; Taylor MLN XXXIII 394ff.; Anderson Journal of English and Germanic Philology XLVI 367—82; Braddy California Folklore Quarterly IV 82f.; Bagatti Franciscan Studies IX 1—9.—Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 105 No. 933; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 778*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 754*.
Q502.1.p: The Wandering Jew: a man is condemned to wander ceaselessly and cannot die as punishment for blasphemy.

Q502.2.r: *Types 400, 425; *BP II 272; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 4.
Q502.2.p: Punishment in which a person must keep wandering until his iron shoes are worn out.

Q502.3.p: A tribe must wander for a long time in the wilderness as a punishment.

Q503.p: Punishment in which the dead must wander after death.

Q503.1.r: Man uses the skull to kill an owl that was about to kill a rabbit; thus after 777 years of rolling it has saved a life and is freed. (Cf. Q211.5.) Köhler-Bolte I 406.
Q503.1.p: The skull of a suicide must roll in the dust until it has saved a life.

Q511.r: (Cf. Q211.) RTP II 267, VIII 586; FL IX 375ff. No. 3; Zs. f. österreichische Volkskunde VII 197; Irish myth: *Cross.
Q511.p: Punishment in which the sufferer must carry the corpse of a murdered man.

Q511.1.r: This is to be put on the grave. Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 72, Cross.
Q511.1.p: A murderer must carry the corpse until a stone as long as the murdered man is found.

Q511.2.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 66 No. 9.
Q511.2.p: A murderer must carry the corpse until he can persuade someone else to take it from him.

Q512.p: A punishment in which the offender is made to do a task that cannot possibly be finished, so the suffering never ends.

Q512.0.1.p: A murderer is punished by being set an impossible task to perform.

Q512.1.p: The offender must keep filling leaking vessels with water drawn from a jar that has no bottom, so the vessels never fill.

Q512.2.p: The offender is punished by being made to bind sand together with string, a task that can never succeed.

Q512.3.p: The offender is punished by being made to rid the country of pests, a task that can never be completed.

Q520.r: *Types 756ABC; *BP III 463; **Andrejev FFC LIV, LXIX 126ff., 234ff.; *Toldo II 87; Irish: Beal XXI 316, *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
Q520.p: Penance is a religious or moral punishment in which a wrongdoer must perform a hard act of atonement to make amends.

Q520.0.1.p: Instead of doing a penance themselves, a person is allowed to offer a substitute or stand-in to perform it.

Q520.1.r: (Cf. Q171.1.1, Q211.) *Types 756BC; **Andrejev FFC LIV, LXIX 85, 118ff., 238ff.; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
Q520.1.p: A murderer must perform a penance as atonement for the killing.

Q520.2.r: (Cf. Q212.) *Types 756B; **Andrejev FFC LXIX 81, 118ff., 236ff; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
Q520.2.p: A robber must perform a penance as atonement for the theft or robbery.

Q520.3.p: Someone who married a brother or sister must spend their whole life doing penance for the incestuous marriage.

Q520.4.p: A king who loves giving death sentences accepts a penance that makes him always delay any execution until thirty days of examination have passed.

Q520.5.p: Men who left holy orders to marry must do penance by living alone in the wilderness.

Q520.6.p: A warrior retires to a monastery to do penance, and later he must defend that same monastery against robbers.

Q521.p: Penances that are long, dull, and wearisome, requiring endless repetition of a pointless or impossible action.

Q521.1.r: *Types 756ABC; *BP III 463; **Andrejev FFC LIV 34, LXIX 126, 129ff., 241ff.; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 49; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 79f., Espinosa Jr. No. 186; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 143.
Q521.1.p: The penitent must keep doing a penance until green leaves grow on a dead, dry branch.

Q521.1.1.r: Types 756BC; **Andrejev FFC LIV 34, LXIX 132; *BP III 471 n. 1; Scala Celi 136a No. 755; Alphabet No. 568.
Q521.1.1.p: The penitent crawls on their knees and waters a dry staff, continuing until it blooms.

Q521.1.2.p: The penitent carries water in their mouth from a distance to water a dry staff, continuing until it blooms.

Q521.2.p: The penitent carries a bag of stones on their back, one stone for each murder, until the bag falls off by itself.

Q521.3.p: The penitent carries an iron hoop on their head and must keep doing so until it falls off.

Q521.4.p: The penitent must herd black sheep until they turn white.

Q521.5.p: A penance in which a person must keep ferrying others over a stream, and can stop only when another ferryman takes over.

Q521.6.r: *Sébillot RTP X 584, XIII 179, XV 621; Ireland: Baughman, O’Suilleabhain 27, Beal XXI 308; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 70f.
Q521.6.p: A penance in which a person must keep holding midnight mass until someone agrees to give the responses.

Q521.7.p: A penance that lasts until the seven spires of Benares are ground to powder and rebuilt again.

Q522.p: Penance in which a person inflicts pain or injury on himself as punishment for sin.

Q522.1.p: A penitent who punishes himself by having himself crucified.

Q522.2.p: A penance in which a person kills himself with a wooden knife.

Q522.3.r: *Type 756B; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 127; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 202a; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 44, Beal XXI 316; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
Q522.3.p: A penance in which a person crawls naked through thorns.

Q522.4.p: A pilgrimage made as penance with the hands and loins weighted down with iron.

Q522.5.p: A penance in which an iron band is forged around a man's waist.

Q522.6.p: A penance in which a person hangs head downward for a thousand years over a fire of chaff.

Q522.7.p: A penance in which a person wears a friar's cord directly against bare skin.

Q522.8.p: A penance in which a man wears a huge serpent coiled around his body instead of clothing.

Q523.p: Penances meant to shame or degrade the person doing them.

Q523.1.p: A penance in which a person crawls on his knees all the way to Rome.

Q523.1.1.p: A penance in which a person crawls on his knees to a grave.

Q523.2.p: A penance in which a person goes on all fours like an animal.

Q523.3.r: *Dickson 257 n. 80; English: Wells 136 (Sir Gowther); Irish: Beal XXI 330; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 86 No. 756B.
Q523.3.p: A penance in which a person must eat food that was offered to dogs.

Q523.4.p: A penance in which a person lives as a beggar under the stairs.

Q523.5.p: A penance in which a person plants a garden and offers free hospitality to everyone.

Q523.6.p: A penance in which a person who has killed cats, dogs, or similar animals must hang their bodies up and cover them with grain.

Q523.7.r: (Cf. Q223.) Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 179f., 374.
Q523.7.p: A person must serve someone for seven years as punishment for neglecting their religious duties for seven days. The service is a humiliating penance.

Q523.8.p: As a penance, a person must carry out any service or task that anyone asks of them, however demeaning.

Q523.9.p: As a penance, a king must take off his crown and lick spittle off the ground, a deeply humiliating act.

Q523.10.p: As a penance, a person fasts while dressed in sackcloth and covered in ashes, showing grief and repentance.

Q524.p: A group of penances that are frightening or terrifying to undergo.

Q524.1.p: As a penance, a person must spend a lonely night alone in a cave.

Q524.2.p: As a penance, a person must spend the first night with every corpse brought to a certain church, keeping watch over the dead.

Q525.p: A group of penances that are dangerous to undertake and could cause harm or death.

Q525.1.p: A penance in which a person must stay on a rock in the dashing sea as punishment.

Q526.p: A journey to a holy place is imposed as a penance for wrongdoing.

Q527.p: As a penance, a person must invite one Brahmin (a member of the priestly caste) to dinner every Wednesday.

Q535.p: A group of penances that consist of abstaining from something rather than doing a task.

Q535.1.r: *Krappe Balor 181ff.; *Toldo II 91; *Dickson 255 nn. 76, 77; English: Wells 136 (Sir Gowther); Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 86 No. 756B, Keller.
Q535.1.p: As a penance, a person must stay silent and not speak.

Q535.2.r: Chauvin II 105 No. 68; Bødker Exempler 302 No. 71; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
Q535.2.p: A lioness, whose two cubs were killed, gives up eating meat as penance and lives on grass instead. A jackal has told her he suffered the same loss.

Q535.3.p: As a penance, a person gives up sexual intercourse.

Q535.4.p: As a penance, a person fasts alone, without anyone else fasting with them.

Q537.p: A penance in which a person must resist temptation, especially sexual temptation.

Q537.1.r: (Cf. Q241.) Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XIV 52 (St. Theodora).
Q537.1.p: An adulteress disguises herself as a monk and lives chastely in a monastery as penance.

Q537.2.p: A cleric tests himself by living among beautiful women, and remains chaste.

Q541.p: A penance in which a person must sit or stand in an uncomfortable position for a long time.

Q541.1.p: As a penance, a person must sit in water.

Q541.1.1.p: Adam and Eve must stand in the Jordan and Tigris rivers as a penance for their sin. The motif describes this watery penance.

Q541.2.r: Dh I 228ff.; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 49, Beal XXI 318.
Q541.2.p: As a penance, a person stands in water for forty days.

Q541.3.r: (Cf. Q242, T415.) *Type 933; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 173 to Gonzenbach No. 85; *Baum PMLA XXXI 562 n. 59; *Toldo II 89.
Q541.3.p: Gregory does penance by standing on a stone or pillar, as punishment for committing incest.

Q541.4.p: A penitent keeps himself hanging suspended from two iron hooks placed under his armpits, as a penance.

Q541.5.p: As a penance, a person stands rooted in one spot for ten months with eyes closed while birds build nests in his hair.

Q542.p: As a penance, a person gives all of his earnings to the poor.

Q544.p: As a penance, a person is locked in a cellar or well, and the key is thrown into the water so he cannot get out.

Q545.r: (Cf. Q211.) *Type 756C; **Andrejev FFC LIV; Wesselski Archiv Orientální II 39ff.
Q545.p: A murderer's penance is considered complete once he kills a greater murderer and so prevents a crime.

Q550.p: Supernatural punishments that fall on wrongdoers, sent as miracles or divine retribution.

Q550.1.p: Supernatural signs or wonders occur when a wicked person dies.

Q551.p: Magic events that serve as punishment for wrongdoers.

Q551.1.r: (Cf. Q281.1.) *BP III 167; Köhler-Bolte I 473ff.; *Ward II 664; Herbert III 343; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 437; Irish: Beal XXI 317.
Q551.1.p: An undutiful son is punished when a toad clings to his face.

Q551.1.1.p: As a punishment, a betel nut grows out of a person's knee.

Q551.2.p: As a punishment, an animal's skin grows on a man's back. In the source, he had put on the skin in disguise to cheat others.

Q551.2.1.p: An object magically sticks to a person as punishment for opposing a holy person.

Q551.2.2.p: Objects miraculously stick to a person's hand as punishment for working on a holy day.

Q551.2.3.p: A thief is unable to take the stolen goods off his back, so the burden stays on him.

Q551.2.4.p: The corpse of a man stays stuck to the back of his murderer as punishment.

Q551.2.5.p: A tool used for unlawful work sticks to the hand of the person holding it.

Q551.2.6.p: Sacrilege and blasphemy are punished by objects magically sticking to the offender.

Q551.2.7.p: A priest's concubine is punished by being stuck fast to a stone and unable to rise. She is freed only through prayers and repentance.

Q551.2.8.p: A stingy man is punished when a bundle of fuel (in some versions, a pitcher of lime) sticks to his head.

Q551.2.8.1.p: A greedy rich man's foot gets caught in a church door. He is freed only when he sends money to a beggar.

Q551.3.p: A person is punished by being magically changed into another form.

Q551.3.1.p: Two lovers who have had sex in a temple are transformed into a lion and a lioness as punishment. The note explains that lions were believed not to mate with each other, so the sin could not be repeated.

Q551.3.2.r: (Cf. Q226.2.) S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 31.
Q551.3.2.p: A person is punished by being transformed into an animal.

Q551.3.2.1.p: Loki's son is transformed into a wolf, which then tears his brother to pieces.

Q551.3.2.2.p: A woman is punished by being transformed into a bird.

Q551.3.2.3.p: A person is punished by being transformed into a frog.

Q551.3.2.4.p: A person is punished by being transformed into a monkey.

Q551.3.2.5.p: A man is punished by being transformed into a mass of worms.

Q551.3.2.6.p: A person is punished by being transformed into a donkey.

Q551.3.2.7.p: A person is punished by being transformed into a dog.

Q551.3.2.8.p: A person is punished by being transformed into a calf.

Q551.3.3.p: A murderer is punished when the calf's head he holds turns into the head of the man he killed.

Q551.3.3.1.p: A calf's head in a murderer's hand turns into the head of the murdered man's corpse. The murderer is thus exposed by the magic change.

Q551.3.4.p: A person is punished by being turned to stone.

Q551.3.4.1.p: People who mock a saint are turned to stone by him.

Q551.3.4.2.p: A man who curses the wind is turned to stone, together with the sack he is sowing from.

Q551.3.4.3.p: A nun who breaks her vow is turned to stone as punishment.

Q551.3.5.p: A person is punished by being transformed into some other object, not an animal or stone.

Q551.3.5.1.p: A person is punished by being magically turned into a falling star.

Q551.3.5.2.p: A person is punished by being magically turned into a tree.

Q551.4.p: Animals are punished by a supernatural force that makes them fall sick.

Q551.4.1.p: Horses are punished by a supernatural force that makes them fall sick.

Q551.5.p: A person is punished by being reborn into a new life through magic.

Q551.5.1.p: A person is punished by being reborn in a lower or more degraded form.

Q551.5.1.1.p: A man is punished by being reborn as a girl.

Q551.5.1.2.p: A king and queen are punished by being reborn as the children of a scavenger.

Q551.5.1.3.p: A dying priest who greedily looks at a ripe plum is reborn as an insect that feeds inside a plum.

Q551.6.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 187.
Q551.6.p: A person is punished with a sickness sent by magic.

Q551.6.0.1.p: Men are punished by being struck with leprosy.

Q551.6.0.2.p: A person who obtained food by force from a monastery dies of an unknown disease within three days.

Q551.6.1.p: A person who lies under oath (perjury) is punished with a magic sickness.

Q551.6.2.p: A person who opposes a holy person is punished with a magic sickness.

Q551.6.2.1.p: A person who tans shoes with bark from a saint's tree is punished with a magic sickness.

Q551.6.3.p: A person who is ungrateful is punished with a magic sickness.

Q551.6.4.r: (Cf. Q212, Q557.4, Q572.1.) *Loomis White Magic 98; Irish myth: Cross.
Q551.6.4.p: A thief is punished with a magic sickness.

Q551.6.5.p: A person who desecrates holy places or images is punished with a magic sickness.

Q551.6.5.1.p: A blasphemer suddenly bleeds from the mouth as a magic punishment.

Q551.6.5.2.p: A blasphemer's eyes fall out of his head as a magic punishment.

Q551.6.6.p: A person wastes away to skin and bones because of envy, and this wasting is a magical punishment. The wasting-away is the penalty for envying someone.

Q551.6.7.p: A person who refuses hospitality is struck by a magical sickness that causes death. The sudden illness or death is the punishment for being inhospitable to a guest.

Q551.7.r: Loomis White Magic 98f.; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
Q551.7.p: A person is magically made unable to move, and this paralysis is the punishment. The general idea covers the sub-motifs that specify the offence.

Q551.7.1.p: A person who opposes a holy man is magically paralyzed as punishment for that opposition.

Q551.7.1.1.p: A heretic who speaks against the faith suddenly loses the power of speech and cannot talk. The tongue-tying is the punishment for his heresy.

Q551.7.2.r: (Cf. Q212.) *Loomis White Magic 98; Irish myth: Cross.
Q551.7.2.p: A thief is magically paralyzed as punishment for stealing, so he cannot move or escape.

Q551.7.3.p: A quarrelsome person is magically paralyzed as punishment for constant fighting or arguing.

Q551.8.p: A person is punished with a physical deformity, which is a magical or miraculous penalty. The sub-motifs specify the offence.

Q551.8.1.p: A judge who judges falsely is punished by becoming deformed.

Q551.8.2.p: A person who desecrates a holy place or sacred image is punished with deformity.

Q551.8.3.p: A murderer is punished by his body becoming deformed or rotting while still alive, showing the corruption of his crime.

Q551.8.4.p: A man who urges a saint to marry is punished when one of his eyes bursts out of his head.

Q551.8.5.p: A man who lies to a saint has his head fall off as punishment for the lie.

Q551.8.6.p: A sinner's tongue sticks out of his mouth as a magical punishment, and then he goes blind.

Q551.8.7.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 600, 808.
Q551.8.7.p: A person is punished by having his face twisted or distorted out of shape.

Q551.9.r: (Cf. Q414.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q551.9.p: A person is punished by being miraculously burned. The sub-motifs specify the offence.

Q551.9.1.p: A person who opposes a holy man is punished by being miraculously burned.

Q551.9.2.p: A person who swears falsely under oath is burned to death by magic as punishment for perjury.

Q551.10.p: A blasphemer is lifted miraculously into the air and then dashed to the ground, dying from the fall, as punishment.

Q551.10.1.p: A person who scoffs at church teachings is lifted into the air by magic and dashed to death as punishment.

Q551.11.p: A person is punished by being made to forget everything, through a magical effect. The forgetting itself is the penalty.

Q551.12.p: A person is punished by aging prematurely through magic, becoming old before their time.

Q552.p: A punishment brought about by a wonder or supernatural sign, such as a miraculous event sent to punish someone.

Q552.0.1.p: A poet who has judged unjustly is killed by a natural element, such as fire, water, or wind, as a miraculous punishment.

Q552.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 458; *Blinkenberg The Thunderweapon in Religion and Folklore (Cambridge, Eng., 1911); *P. Saintyves Pierres magiques (Paris, 1936).—Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 336, O’Suilleabhain 123; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 18 Nos. 165, 173; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3267; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 34 n. 2 (Iasion), 52 n. 2 (Asopus); Jewish: *Neuman.
Q552.1.p: A person is punished by being killed by a thunderbolt or lightning.

Q552.1.0.1.p: A person is punished by having their property destroyed by a thunderbolt.

Q552.1.0.1.1.p: A fortress is demolished by a thunderbolt as punishment for its people disobeying a saint.

Q552.1.0.2.p: Thunder kills people who have shown disregard for it or for the one who sends it.

Q552.1.1.r: (Cf. Q331.) Scala Celi 102b No. 152; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 455; Alphabet No. 116.
Q552.1.1.p: A monk who despises humility is struck dead by lightning.

Q552.1.2.p: A man who ravishes (sexually assaults) someone is killed by a thunderbolt.

Q552.1.3.r: (Cf. Q262.) Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 110 No. 65.
Q552.1.3.p: A false pretender or impostor is killed by lightning.

Q552.1.4.p: A person who opposes a holy person is killed by a thunderbolt as punishment.

Q552.1.5.p: A traitor is killed by a thunderbolt as punishment for betrayal.

Q552.1.6.p: A person who acts unjustly is killed by a thunderbolt as punishment.

Q552.1.7.p: A woman who falsely accuses a saint of raping her is struck dead by lightning.

Q552.1.8.p: An unbeliever challenges God to strike him with lightning, and is struck.

Q552.1.8.1.p: A cattle thief calls on God to strike him with lightning if he has ever stolen a cow or calf, and lightning strikes him.

Q552.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 18f. Nos. 164, 188; India: Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 511.
Q552.2.p: The earth sinks and swallows a person or place as a miraculous punishment.

Q552.2.0.1.p: The earth shakes or quakes as a miraculous punishment.

Q552.2.0.1.1.p: The earth quakes whenever a saint is opposed.

Q552.2.1.r: *Fb “sø” III 449b; Loomis White Magic 41, 101; England: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 787*; Chinese: Werner 405.
Q552.2.1.p: The ground sinks and a lake forms in its place as a punishment for wrongdoing.

Q552.2.2.r: (Cf. Q212.2.) Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 116 No. 17.
Q552.2.2.p: A grave sinks into the earth so that thieves who came to rob it cannot climb out.

Q552.2.3.r: (Cf. F940, Q221.4.3.) Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 327, O’Suilleabhain 79; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. 3610, 3748, Legends Nos. 467f., 470f; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Q552.2.3.p: A person or thing is punished by being swallowed up by the earth.

Q552.2.3.1.p: A girl is swallowed into the ground up to her body for dancing in church.

Q552.2.3.1.1.r: (Cf. Q227.) Loomis White Magic 44; Irish myth: *Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 798, II 1220.
Q552.2.3.1.1.p: The earth swallows a man who opposes a holy man or saint.

Q552.2.3.1.2.p: The earth swallows a man as punishment for blasphemy, heresy, or other sacrilege.

Q552.2.3.1.3.p: A man who angers a saint sinks into the ground up to his knees.

Q552.2.3.2.p: The earth swallows an object as punishment.

Q552.2.3.2.1.p: The earth swallows a mill after its owner refuses to let a saint's grain be ground there.

Q552.2.3.2.2.p: The earth swallows a city whose people are heretics.

Q552.2.3.2.3.p: An island sinks into the sea as punishment for a man's offense against a saint.

Q552.2.3.3.p: A saint causes a man who committed parricide, killing his father or mother, to sink into the earth up to his knees.

Q552.2.3.4.p: The earth swallows a man who intends to commit treachery.

Q552.3.r: (Cf. Q552.10.1.) Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 72, *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Grote I 171, 203; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Q552.3.p: Crops fail during the reign of a wicked king, as a punishment on the land.

Q552.3.0.1.p: Crops fail as punishment for lack of charity or refusal to help others.

Q552.3.0.2.p: Crops fail as punishment for murder.

Q552.3.0.3.p: Crops and milk fail as punishment for adultery.

Q552.3.0.4.p: Crops fail as punishment for mistreating the dead.

Q552.3.1.r: *Loomis White Magic 95, 102; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q552.3.1.p: A famine comes as punishment for wrongdoing.

Q552.3.1.1.p: The land becomes barren and unable to grow crops as punishment for killing one's parent.

Q552.3.2.p: A land suffers famine as punishment for the oppression its victorious rulers inflict on the people.

Q552.3.3.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q552.3.3.p: A drought is sent as a punishment, so that no rain falls and the land dries up.

Q552.3.4.p: Food vanishes by magic, leaving people without anything to eat, as a punishment.

Q552.3.5.p: Streams of sugar, molasses, and milk flowing from an anchorite's tomb dry up and turn to stone because the townspeople were greedy.

Q552.3.6.p: A water famine is inflicted as a punishment, so that water becomes scarce.

Q552.3.7.p: A murrain, a deadly disease, strikes the cattle as a punishment.

Q552.4.r: (Cf. Q212.) Irish: Plummer cxliii, *Cross; *Loomis White Magic 98.
Q552.4.p: A thief who has stolen an animal is punished when the animal's ear sticks out of his mouth.

Q552.4.1.p: A thief who has eaten a stolen animal is exposed when the animal cries out from inside his stomach.

Q552.5.r: (Cf. M437, Q331, T550.) Child I 210; Ireland, U.S.: Baughman.
Q552.5.p: A girl who is proud is punished when she gives birth to monstrous children.

Q552.5.1.r: (Cf. Q285.1.1.) Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 19 No. 182; Japanese: Ikeda.
Q552.5.1.p: A man who cuts out the tongue of a swallow is punished when his own children are born unable to speak.

Q552.6.p: A rich lord who steals a poor widow's cow chokes on the first mouthful of food he eats.

Q552.7.p: An image of the Virgin Mary comes down from its place and punishes a clerk who mocks its crude carving.

Q552.8.p: A dead rooster rises, crows, and splatters those who scoffed at it, and they become leprous.

Q552.9.p: A woman who has prevented the birth of children is punished by casting no shadow.

Q552.10.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 165; German: O. Busch Nordwestthüringer Sagen 145, E. Handreck Müllersagen 194, O. Schöppner Sagenbuch d. bairischen Lande I 72; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
Q552.10.p: A plague is sent as a punishment on a people or land.

Q552.10.1.p: Plague keeps returning during the reign of a wicked king, as punishment.

Q552.11.r: (Ghost, mysterious animal, devil.) Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 17ff. Nos. 158—161, 167, 169-71, 179.
Q552.11.p: A person is punished by coming face to face with a frightful apparition.

Q552.12.p: A ship is wrecked as a punishment.

Q552.13.p: Fire falls from heaven as a punishment, burning the guilty.

Q552.13.0.1.p: Punishment is inflicted by arrows of fire shot down from heaven.

Q552.13.0.2.p: A flaming sword descends from heaven and strikes sinners as a punishment from God.

Q552.13.0.3.p: The gods pour showers of hot ashes onto a kingdom as a punishment.

Q552.13.1.p: A person is killed by fire sent down from heaven as a punishment.

Q552.13.1.1.p: A person who opposes a holy man is killed by fire from heaven as a punishment.

Q552.13.1.2.p: A person who mocks church teachings is killed by fire from heaven as a punishment.

Q552.13.2.p: Property is destroyed by fire from heaven as a punishment.

Q552.13.2.1.p: The city of a king who opposed a saint is miraculously burned as a punishment.

Q552.13.2.2.p: A church that refuses to bury a saint is miraculously burned as a punishment.

Q552.13.3.p: Fire from heaven consumes an adulterous wife who has slandered an abbot.

Q552.14.p: A storm is sent as a punishment.

Q552.14.0.1.r: (Cf. Q221.) S. A. Indian (Chamacoco): Métraux MAFLS XL 28.
Q552.14.0.1.p: A storm is sent as a punishment for insulting a disguised supernatural spirit.

Q552.14.1.p: A fortress that was built on a Sunday is destroyed by a tempest.

Q552.14.2.p: As a punishment, a flood of mud comes, and afterward the corn grows with black, smutted ears.

Q552.14.3.p: A mass of sand sweeps forward like a tidal wave onto a city.

Q552.14.4.p: A rain of stones falls as a punishment.

Q552.15.p: As a punishment, a cloud blocks a man's view of the land he was promised for expelling a saint, so he cannot see all that was offered.

Q552.16.p: Food and drink refused to a saint miraculously turn rotten.

Q552.16.1.p: Food hidden from a saint is miraculously changed into stones.

Q552.16.1.1.p: Fishermen cut their fish into pieces and claim they have none; the saint curses them, and the fish pieces turn to stones.

Q552.16.1.2.p: Women hide cheeses under their clothes and pretend they are carrying webs or balls of thread. A saint turns the hidden cheeses to stone as punishment for the deception.

Q552.17.p: A man digging a grave for a sinner, who is to be buried over a holy man, finds the hole filling with sand every time he tries to dig it. The miracle prevents the sinner from being buried there.

Q552.18.r: (Cf. Q585, Q595.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
Q552.18.p: A person who has gained wealth dishonestly loses it through a miracle, which punishes them.

Q552.18.1.p: Gold and silver that someone demands from a saint vanish, so the demand is punished.

Q552.18.1.1.p: A cowl (monk's hood) that someone demands as ransom from a saint bursts into flames.

Q552.18.2.p: Someone refuses a drink offered by a saint, and then the person disappears as punishment.

Q552.18.3.p: A ransom payment for a prisoner vanishes when the prisoner is not released.

Q552.19.r: (Cf. Q428, Q467.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
Q552.19.p: A person is drowned by a miracle as a punishment.

Q552.19.0.1.p: A braggart is drowned by a wind produced by magic, as punishment for boasting.

Q552.19.1.r: (Cf. Q227.) Irish myth: *Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 1042.
Q552.19.1.p: A person who opposes a saint or holy man is drowned miraculously as punishment.

Q552.19.2.p: A person who wishes to murder someone is drowned miraculously as punishment for that desire.

Q552.19.3.p: A thief is drowned miraculously as punishment for stealing.

Q552.19.4.p: A man who runs off with his stepmother is drowned miraculously as punishment.

Q552.19.5.p: A proud, arrogant person is drowned miraculously as punishment for haughtiness.

Q552.19.6.p: A flood is sent as punishment for a murder, specifically the killing of a brother.

Q552.20.p: A solar or lunar eclipse is sent as a punishment.

Q552.20.1.p: Darkness is sent miraculously as a punishment.

Q552.21.p: A man is punished by having his heart vomited out, and he lives on without it until he dies.

Q552.22.p: A city and its inhabitants are hurled down a precipice as punishment.

Q552.23.p: A person is punished by being suspended in the air between heaven and earth.

Q552.24.p: A lava flow is sent as a punishment for wrongdoing, a miraculous judgment in which molten rock destroys or overwhelms the offenders.

Q552.25.p: An earthquake is sent as a punishment for wrongdoing, a miraculous judgment in which the ground shakes to punish the guilty.

Q552.25.1.p: An earthquake occurs when a dragon dies.

Q552.25.2.p: An earthquake occurs when a witch dies.

Q553.p: God or the divine withdraws its favor or help from someone as a punishment, so that the person loses blessings they once had.

Q553.1.p: The Virgin Mary takes away the sacrament from a person who mocks it, so that the scoffer no longer receives communion.

Q553.2.r: Type 756A; Köhler-Bolte I 147f., 578; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 81, Espinosa Jr. No. 186.
Q553.2.p: As a punishment, an angel stops appearing to a hermit who has become self-righteous and proud of his holiness.

Q553.3.p: A person or couple is made unable to have children as a punishment from God or a saint.

Q553.3.0.1.p: Women are made sterile, unable to bear children, as a punishment.

Q553.3.1.p: God refuses a king a son because the king has fought many wars.

Q553.3.2.p: The children of a father who committed incest die without leaving descendants.

Q553.3.3.r: (Cf. Q227.) Irish myth: Cross; Greek (Herodotus): Classical Philology 39 (1944) 179f.
Q553.3.3.p: A couple is made sterile as punishment for breaking a covenant made with a saint.

Q553.3.4.p: A person who has killed a parent is made sterile as a punishment.

Q553.3.5.p: A person is made sterile as punishment for being unkind or uncharitable to a holy person.

Q553.3.6.p: Children are born only with great pain to the mother as a punishment.

Q553.3.7.p: As a punishment, a person is given fewer children than they would otherwise have had.

Q553.4.p: A person's children are killed or taken away from them as a punishment.

Q553.4.1.p: A child is taken from the parents because the parents have stopped thinking about God.

Q553.5.p: A fisherman and his wife, who killed their child out of greed for more fish, are punished by catching fewer fish afterward. Before the murder they always caught three fish; afterward they catch only two.

Q553.6.r: Loomis White Magic 100; Jewish: Moreno Esdras (Q479.1); India: Thompson-Balys.
Q553.6.p: A person fails in everything they attempt as a punishment from God or another power.

Q553.7.p: Rain is held back because a king has failed to keep his promise to have the roofs of the monks' huts repaired. The rain returns only once he fulfills the promise.

Q554.p: A strange, supernatural visitation that comes as a punishment for wrongdoing.

Q554.1.p: The devil comes and carries off a thief as punishment for stealing.

Q554.2.p: The devil hides in a church roof and pushes the voices of loud singers into himself, punishing them for singing so loudly.

Q554.3.p: A mysterious stranger blows ashes into the face of a mocker, choking him to death.

Q554.4.p: A mysterious wolf enters a church and kills a priest who has been blaspheming.

Q554.5.r: (Cf. Q557.) Köhler-Bolte I 132; Euphorion IV 332; Irish: Beal XXI 317, O’Suilleabhain 46; Gascon: Bladé Contes pop. de Gascogne II 201 No. 13.
Q554.5.p: A man who has repented is attacked by a mysterious animal that jumps on his back. In his room a fight is heard for three hours, yet neither man nor beast is found there afterward.

Q554.6.p: People who have cheated others are visited by God in the form of an animal, which frightens them into giving back what they took.

Q554.7.p: A creditor from a past life comes back in the next life to seize the wealth of an unkind man.

Q555.r: (Cf. D2065.) *Loomis White Magic 98; Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 146 n. 2, 183 n. 3; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Q555.p: Madness sent as a punishment for wrongdoing.

Q555.1.p: A mocker is punished by being driven mad.

Q555.2.r: (Cf. Q241.) Alphabet No. 36; Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Aeschylus Eumenides 341.
Q555.2.p: An adulterer is punished by being driven mad.

Q555.3.p: Thieves are punished by being driven mad.

Q555.4.p: For incest, a father and son are driven mad, and their sexual organs are cut off.

Q556.r: Roberts 217; Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 83, Beal XXI 328; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q556.p: A curse placed on someone as a punishment.

Q556.0.1.p: A curse is threatened to force someone to meet a demand.

Q556.0.2.p: A voice from heaven pronounces a curse of destruction upon a city.

Q556.1.p: Those who took part in the Crucifixion of Jesus are cursed as punishment.

Q556.2.r: (Cf. Q211.) *Frazer Old Testament I 78ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
Q556.2.p: A permanent mark is placed on a murderer as a curse, like the Mark of Cain.

Q556.3.p: A person is cursed for leaving home.

Q556.4.p: A person who disobeys a saint is cursed to take on the pale, deathlike color of a corpse.

Q556.4.1.p: A child is born with one eye blinded because of a saint's curse.

Q556.5.r: (Cf. D2192, Q227, Q552.) Irish myth: Cross.
Q556.5.p: A saint declares that the offenders will never be able to make their homes secure: fences collapse and the ground splits open when they try to dig.

Q556.6.p: A king who plunders a church is cursed so that he keeps losing his battles.

Q556.7.p: A person who refuses hospitality to a holy person or traveler is punished by a curse.

Q556.7.1.p: A person who is forced to offer hospitality is punished by a curse.

Q556.8.p: A person who mocks a saint or holy figure is punished with a curse.

Q556.9.p: A man who banishes his wife at the urging of his lover is cursed for it.

Q556.10.p: A person who commits murder is cursed by a saint.

Q556.10.1.p: A saint curses a murderer so that he will have a short life on earth and suffer in hell afterward.

Q556.11.p: A person who is uncharitable or refuses to give to others is punished by a curse.

Q556.12.p: A thief is punished with a curse.

Q556.12.1.p: A thieving abbot is cursed by a saint so that wolves will eat him.

Q557.p: A wrongdoer is punished by a miracle carried out through animals.

Q557.1.p: A poisonous toad sits on the food of children who are disobedient to their parents.

Q557.2.p: A serpent chokes the undutiful son of a woman.

Q557.3.p: An eagle, or in some versions an ape, snatches away ill-gotten money.

Q557.4.p: A mouse makes a thief's hair fall out.

Q557.5.p: A saint's pet crane pecks out the eye of a person who is spying.

Q557.6.p: A snake strikes a person who opposes a saint.

Q557.7.p: A tiger attacks a newly married couple at the doorway of their home because the groom did not first pay worship to a god before the wedding. The animal seizes them as a punishment for this neglect.

Q557.8.p: People are given a charm to drive away flies, but they complain about it, and as a punishment the flies come back a thousand times over.

Q558.p: A general heading for punishments in which someone is struck dead in a mysterious, supernatural way rather than by ordinary means.

Q558.1.p: A priest who mocks or scoffs at sacred matters suddenly dies in a mysterious way as punishment.

Q558.2.r: (Cf. Q263.) Icelandic: Boberg; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 19 No. 177.
Q558.2.p: A person who swears falsely under oath is suddenly struck dead as punishment.

Q558.3.p: A moneylender flees his town to escape a plague. When he returns he boasts that God did not catch him, and then he catches the plague and dies.

Q558.4.r: (Cf. Q221.3.) England: Baughman; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller (Q221.3.3); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
Q558.4.p: A person who curses or speaks blasphemously against God or sacred things is suddenly struck dead.

Q558.5.p: A man, angry, throws a stone at an image of the Virgin Mary and is then struck dead for the act.

Q558.6.p: A thief suffers a mysterious, supernatural death as punishment for stealing.

Q558.7.p: A cruel slave-driver who abuses his workers is suddenly and mysteriously struck dead.

Q558.8.p: A person who satirizes or mocks others unjustly is struck dead by a mysterious power as punishment.

Q558.9.p: A murderer suffers a mysterious, supernatural death as punishment for killing someone.

Q558.9.1.p: A murderer's son dies mysteriously as punishment for the father's killing.

Q558.10.p: A person who pretends to be asleep in order to spy or deceive is suddenly struck dead as punishment.

Q558.11.p: Animals that eat the body of a saint are suddenly struck dead as punishment.

Q558.12.p: A person who worships idols on All Saints' Day is struck dead by a mysterious power as punishment.

Q558.13.p: A person who opposes or insults a holy person is suddenly struck dead as punishment.

Q558.13.1.p: The son of a person who opposed a holy man dies mysteriously as punishment for that opposition.

Q558.13.2.p: A person who refuses to believe in druidism, the ancient Celtic religion, is struck dead as punishment.

Q558.14.p: A person who desecrates or defiles holy places, such as shrines or images, is suddenly struck dead as punishment.

Q558.14.1.p: Animals are struck dead as punishment for desecrating holy places, such as sacred images or shrines.

Q558.15.p: A person who lies under oath, or commits perjury, dies in a mysterious, supernatural way as punishment.

Q558.15.1.p: A person's son dies mysteriously as punishment for that person's lying or perjury.

Q558.16.p: A judge who gives a false judgment dies in a mysterious, supernatural way as punishment.

Q558.17.p: A person who destroys churches dies of an ulcer as punishment.

Q558.18.p: Saints cause a miraculous death as punishment for someone who desecrates a sanctuary.

Q559.p: A general heading for other miraculous punishments that supernatural beings inflict on wrongdoers, apart from sudden death.

Q559.1.r: U.S., England: Baughman; Russian: Andrejev No. 796*.
Q559.1.p: A woman who has become proud and forgotten God in her prosperity is visited by devils disguised as angels instead of real angels.

Q559.2.r: (Cf. Q451.7.0.2.) Irish: Beal XXI 336; Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 18 No. 172; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Q559.2.p: A man is punished by being struck blind.

Q559.3.p: A murdered man's body cannot be moved, and water cannot be drawn from a well to wash it, which leads to the murderer being exposed.

Q559.4.p: Peasants who work on a holy feast day are punished by being unable to leave the field for several days.

Q559.5.p: A girl who jeers at a saint is punished by becoming mute, and her distaff sticks to her hand.

Q559.5.1.p: A girl's pregnancy cannot result in a birth until she confesses that she slandered a bishop by claiming he fathered her child.

Q559.5.2.p: A girl's hand withers as punishment for breaking an oath made to God.

Q559.6.p: Poets lose their ability to compose verse as punishment for making an immoderate request.

Q559.7.p: A man who breaks a saint's covenant is punished by having his body not decay after death.

Q559.8.p: Half of the house where a false judgment was given slips down a hill.

Q559.9.p: Saints miraculously cause a child to fall over a cliff as punishment for the mother washing clothes in a holy well.

Q559.10.p: A magic boat keeps a thief at sea until he promises to throw his stolen goods into the sea.

Q559.11.p: A man is miraculously made to excrete his own entrails as punishment for heresy.

Q560.r: (Cf. Q174.) Fb “helvede” IV 209a; Wienert FFC LVI 41; Krappe “Notes on Dante’s Inferno” Archivum Romanicum VI 376—385, XI 592—603; Festskrift til Feilberg 202. — Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 319—23, O’Suilleabhain 51, 53, 58; Icelandic: *Boberg; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 391, 467f., 470f., 585; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 202, 204, Keller; Greek: Grote I 129; Egyptian: Müller 179f.; Jewish: *Neuman, Moreno Esdras; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 598.
Q560.p: Sinners are punished in hell, in various kinds of torment.

Q560.1.p: A detailed account of the punishments that await the wicked in the land of the dead or the other world.

Q560.1.1.p: In the other world, wrongdoers are reborn as buffaloes and then killed.

Q560.2.p: Tormented souls are given a break from the torments of hell.

Q560.2.1.p: Souls in hell are not punished on the Sabbath, so they get a day of rest.

Q560.2.1.1.p: Those tormented in hell get three hours of relief on Sunday.

Q560.2.2.p: A certain number of souls are let out of hell every Saturday because of a saint's merit.

Q560.2.3.p: The soul of Judas is tormented on a rock in the sea on certain days, which serves as a respite from the pains of hell.

Q560.3.p: Sinners suffer the torments of hell for a period of one year.

Q561.p: Punishments are being prepared in hell for particular people before they arrive.

Q561.1.r: *Type 756B; **Andrejev FFC LXIX 106ff.; *Fb “seng” III 187a; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 391.
Q561.1.p: A bed is being heated in hell for a particular person, to torment them.

Q561.2.p: A kettle is being heated in hell for a particular person.

Q561.3.r: *Type 756B; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 106ff.; Irish: Beal XXI 311, O’Suilleabhain 33.
Q561.3.p: A seat or room is being heated in hell for a particular person.

Q561.4.p: In the other world of the dead there is a palace with rooms full of the tongues, hands and other body parts of people who sinned on earth.

Q562.p: The pain of souls tormented in hell rises and falls in alternating waves rather than staying constant.

Q562.1.p: The girdles worn by sinners in hell alternately scorch them with heat and chill them with cold.

Q562.2.p: Souls in hell are alternately drowned and burned.

Q562.3.p: Souls in hell are alternately lifted up to the firmament and thrown down into the depths.

Q563.r: (Cf. Q580.) Zs. f. celtische Phil. IX 413ff.; Irish myth: *Cross.
Q563.p: The punishments in hell are matched to the sins the person committed.

Q563.1.p: The punishment in hell is matched to how wicked a person was.

Q564.p: A man punished in hell sends a letter back to his living relatives, usually to warn them or ask for help.

Q565.r: *Type 330; *BP II 149ff., 163ff.; Fb “helvede” I 589a, “himmerige” I 611a; Irish: Beal XXI 329, O’Suilleabhain 90; U.S.: *Baughman; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 8, 210, 213; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 156 No. 32.
Q565.p: A man is refused entry to both heaven and hell, usually because he has outwitted the devil.

Q565.1.p: A person is turned away by both the earth and heaven, so has nowhere to go after death.

Q566.r: (Cf. A671.2.4.) Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 885.
Q566.p: Sinners in hell are punished by heat, such as burning or fire.

Q567.r: *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 18; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
Q567.p: Sinners in hell are punished by cold, such as freezing.

Q567.1.p: Sinners in hell are made to wear sharp, icy hoods or cowls that cut or torment them.

Q569.p: A miscellaneous group of other torments inflicted on sinners in hell.

Q569.1.p: Sinners in hell are made to sit in dark, filthy puddles reaching up to their waists.

Q569.2.p: Sinners in hell are swallowed by dragons.

Q569.3.p: Sinners in hell fall into the mouth of the devil.

Q569.4.p: Sinners in hell are hung up and suspended in painful positions.

Q569.5.p: People who smoked in life are locked in smoke-filled rooms in the otherworld.

Q570.p: A punishment is lifted or forgiven, often after a prayer, a plea, or a good deed.

Q570.1.p: A magic foul disease sent as punishment for persecuting Christians is lifted when the persecution stops or is forgiven.

Q571.p: A magically caused blindness inflicted as punishment is lifted or forgiven.

Q571.1.r: (Cf. Q227.) O’Grady Silva Gadelica II 7; Irish myth: *Cross.
Q571.1.p: A magical blindness punishing someone for opposing a holy person is lifted.

Q571.2.p: A magical blindness punishing someone for being uncharitable is lifted.

Q572.p: A magically caused sickness inflicted as punishment is lifted or forgiven.

Q572.1.r: (Cf. Q212.) O’Grady Silva Gadelica II 37; Irish myth: Cross.
Q572.1.p: A magical sickness punishing someone for theft is lifted.

Q572.2.p: A magical sickness punishing someone for being uncharitable is lifted.

Q572.3.p: A holy person's opponent is struck with a magic sickness as punishment, and the sickness is lifted when the opponent makes amends. The punishment is forgiven.

Q572.4.p: Someone who makes an excessive or unreasonable demand is hit with a magic sickness as punishment, and the sickness is later lifted.

Q572.5.p: A saint takes away the speech of an enemy king. The king repents and his speech is restored.

Q573.p: A magic paralysis is inflicted as punishment, and the punishment is later forgiven or lifted.

Q573.1.r: Cf. O’Grady Silva Gadelica II 28; Irish myth: Cross.
Q573.1.p: A person who opposes a holy person is magically paralyzed as punishment, and the paralysis is lifted.

Q573.2.p: A person who scorns a bishop is magically paralyzed as punishment, and the paralysis is later lifted.

Q574.p: Someone dies in a mysterious way as punishment, and the death is later undone or forgiven.

Q574.1.r: (Cf. Q558.13.) O’Grady Silva Gadelica II 71; Irish myth: *Cross.
Q574.1.p: A person who opposes a holy person dies mysteriously as punishment, and the punishment is lifted.

Q574.2.p: Animals die mysteriously as punishment for lack of charity, and the punishment is later lifted.

Q575.r: (Cf. Q227.) O’Grady Silva Gadelica II 26; Irish myth: Cross.
Q575.p: Food is magically spoiled and rots as punishment for opposing a holy person, and the punishment is later lifted.

Q576.p: A curse is imposed as punishment, and the curse is later lifted or forgiven.

Q576.1.p: A person who opposes a holy person is cursed to lose victory in battle, and the curse is lifted.

Q577.p: A sentence of hanging is pardoned or called off.

Q578.p: A spirit in hell is spared from a humiliating punishment of having people bathe in it or over it, and the punishment is lifted.

Q580.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; West Indies: Flowers 570.
Q580.p: A punishment is chosen to match the crime, so that the wrongdoer suffers in a way that fits what he did.

Q581.r: *Cox 503 and passim (under head “villain nemesis”); *Fb “dom” IV 101b; *Wesselski Theorie 139; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 64 to Gonzenbach No. 13; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 116; Wienert FFC LVI 49 (ET 83), 51 (ET 109, 110), 59 (ET 199), 132 (ST 382), 135 (ST 406, 447); Halm Aesop Nos. 18, 326.—Irish myth: *Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 2, III No. 10, V Nos. 8, 9; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q581.p: A villain is condemned to the very punishment he had suggested for others and so suffers his own proposed penalty.

Q581.0.1.p: A traitor loses his life because of his own treachery.

Q581.1.r: Scottish: Campbell-Mckay No. 17; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q581.1.p: A person who commits an unusual murder is killed in the same unusual way by the victim's avenger.

Q581.2.p: A villain hiding from his victim is killed by a blow that was aimed at the victim.

Q581.3.p: People who plan to drown others are themselves drowned.

Q581.3.1.p: A person who plans to drown others is himself drowned, so the punishment matches the crime.

Q582.r: (Cf. Q411, D2060.) Irish: O’Suilleabhain 125, Beal XXI 336; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 374, II 851, 1353; Africa (Duala): Lederbogen JAS IV 61, (Wakweli): Bender 106f.
Q582.p: A general heading for punishments where the way a wrongdoer dies mirrors the wrong they committed.

Q582.1.r: Revue Celtique XVI 76; Irish myth: Cross.
Q582.1.p: Two sisters throw a unique jewel into a lake, and they are killed and thrown into the lake after it.

Q582.2.p: A man who brings fire into his house at the devil's urging is burned to death in it.

Q582.3.p: A murderer is killed with his own spear.

Q582.3.1.p: A man is killed by a piece of stone that flies off the rock his victim is dying on, under the murderer's own spear-type justice.

Q582.4.p: A man dies from a single drop of blood from a pet hound he has killed.

Q582.5.p: A man boasts that he fears a saint no more than a hornless sheep, and is later killed by a hornless sheep.

Q582.6.p: A woman is killed by a horse, which is a fitting end for her immoderate request.

Q582.7.p: A boy who threw stones at clerics is killed by a stone thrown at him.

Q582.8.p: A person drinks the poison he had prepared for someone else.

Q582.9.p: A man falls dead on seeing all of his sons, whom he raised in sin, killed.

Q583.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 16.
Q583.p: A general heading for punishments in which the wrongdoer is bodily injured in a way that matches the offense.

Q583.1.p: A man who laughs at a blind person is made blind himself.

Q583.2.p: A man is struck dumb (unable to speak) for rude, surly speech.

Q583.3.p: A man who tries to flee from a saint is paralyzed.

Q583.4.p: A lying woman's tongue swells up as punishment.

Q584.p: A general heading for punishments in which the wrongdoer is transformed in a way that fits the offense.

Q584.1.p: A person who transforms others is himself transformed, so the punishment turns back on the transformer.

Q584.2.r: (Cf. D661.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 773*; S. A. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 133, 172.
Q584.2.p: A man is transformed into an animal as a fitting punishment for his wrongdoing.

Q584.3.r: (Cf. Q551.5.) Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 50, 829, 1020, II 706, 1050, 1357.
Q584.3.p: A person is reborn in a form that matches the crime they committed, as a punishment. The creature they become reflects their wrongdoing.

Q585.r: (Cf. Q552.18, Q595.) India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 885, II 416, 1264.
Q585.p: A person's property vanishes as a punishment that fits their wrong, such as a stingy or wasteful act.

Q585.1.r: (Cf. Q286, Q595.3.) Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
Q585.1.p: A man who refuses to give to charity finds that his own property disappears.

Q585.2.p: Someone who asks for something excessively or greedily loses their property as a result.

Q585.3.p: In a rainy spring a farmer wishes the Lord would sleep until harvest time. The farmer sleeps until the neighbors have finished harvesting, then wakes to find his own crops ruined.

Q585.4.p: Food disappears as a punishment for wasting it.

Q586.r: *Types 756B, 838; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 88; Wienert FFC LVI 83 (ET 493), 128 (ST 365, 499); Halm Aesop No. 351; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 19; Crane Vitry 259 No. 287; *Chauvin VIII 113 No. 95 n. 1; Alphabet No. 217. — Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
Q586.p: A son hanged on the gallows bites off his mother's or father's nose. It is a punishment for having neglected the parent in his youth.

Q587.r: (Laüstic.) *Warncke Lais der Marie de France@2 cxxvi.
Q587.p: A jealous husband kills a bird after his wife falsely tells him she has been listening to it. In fact she has been talking with her lover.

Q588.p: An ungrateful son is punished by having a son who is just as ungrateful to him.

Q589.p: A miscellaneous group of punishments that fit the crime, not covered by more specific headings.

Q589.1.p: A horse or horses fail to pull their load when the owner refuses to share the load with a saint.

Q589.1.0.1.p: A man is unable to drive his cow by himself after refusing to share it with someone.

Q589.2.p: A man who goes out naked is cursed to remain naked for the rest of his life.

Q589.3.p: A stingy person must make amends by becoming generous and liberal.

Q590.p: A miscellaneous group of punishments not classed under the more specific punishment headings.

Q591.r: (Cf. Q263.) *Loomis White Magic 100; Irish: Beal XXI 327, O’Suilleabhain 74; Japanese: Ikeda.
Q591.p: A lie told as a punishment becomes true: the words the liar speaks come to pass.

Q591.1.p: A pretended death becomes a real one: someone who feigns being dead is punished by actually dying.

Q591.1.1.p: A king tests a saint by having a man pretend to be dead. The saint sees through the trick and makes the man really dead.

Q591.2.p: A man says the salt he carries is stones, and it immediately turns into stones as a punishment for his lie.

Q591.2.1.p: A man says the sugar he carries is earth, and it turns into earth as a punishment for his lie.

Q591.3.p: A person pretends to be ill, and the pretence becomes real, so the person dies from the illness they feigned.

Q593.p: A child who disobeys a dead mother is made by her ghost to eat a deadly snake, as punishment.

Q594.p: As a punishment, a person is made to take snakes in as foster children.

Q595.r: (Cf. Q552.1.0.1, Q552.13.2, Q552.14.1, Q585, Q552.18.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Africa (Fang): Tessman 195.
Q595.p: A person is punished by having their property lost or destroyed.

Q595.1.p: A fortress is ravaged and destroyed after a holy man (saint) is refused entry to it.

Q595.2.p: As punishment for an abduction, the abductor's cattle are killed and their crops burned.

Q595.3.p: A stingy king who refuses to give charity loses his wealth as a punishment.

Q595.4.p: A person is punished by losing money.

Q595.4.1.p: As punishment for a trick played on someone, the trickster is made to pay tribute.

Q596.p: A punishment is carried out on a figure or image standing in for the guilty person.

Q596.1.p: A man who has killed his wife is punished by being quartered in effigy, meaning his likeness is torn into quarters.

Q597.p: Animals take revenge on a person who has harmed them.

Q597.1.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 46 No. 79; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 132 No. 79.
Q597.1.p: A snake carries into a fire a man who had forbidden snakes, so he is punished by the fire.

Q597.2.r: (Cf. Q281.) Cape Verde Islands: *Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 310 n. 1; West Indies: Flowers 570.
Q597.2.p: Birds reclaim the feathers they had lent to a wolf, because the wolf was ungrateful to them.

Q597.3.r: (Cf. Q212.) Wienert FFC LVI *67 (ET 312), 98 (ST 122); Halm Aesop No. 288.
Q597.3.p: Bees sting people who steal their honey.

Q598.p: A punishment in which a person must fight everyone who passes through a forest.

Q599.p: A miscellaneous punishment that does not fit the other categories.

Q599.1.p: A man is punished by being forced to marry a nagging, quarrelsome wife.
